E1166.summary: A commentator cited by Atwood for his commentary on an enigmatic epitaph, printed in the Theatrum Chemicum.
E1166.body: Cited as having commented on the epitaph discussed in the text [I.1 ¶24]; the footnote names his commentary in the Theatrum Chemicum, *Commentariolum in Enigmaticum quoddam Epitaphium Bononiae studiorum* [I.1 n32].

E1167.summary: The Name that, Atwood says, we have no business to speak; if it speaks in us, it works its own change.
E1167.body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), insists: “We have no business whatsoever to speak The Name.” [APP ¶88] Her point, as the record gives it, is that it is not for us to utter; if it speaks in us, it works its own change [APP ¶88].

E1168.summary: The soul's bond in life, which she must give up, with dread, during the transition.
E1168.body: Atwood speaks of the soul about to “relinquish her natal bond in life” [II.3 ¶37]. The record glosses it as the soul's bond in life, which she gives up with dread during the transition.

E1169.summary: A figure who, the text says, would not teach Agrippa despite his entreaties.
E1169.body: Cited as having refused to teach Agrippa despite his entreaties [IV.1 ¶36].

E1170.summary: That through which the impure Instrument is brought and returned; the wording also suggests the Instrument then itself constitutes it.
E1170.body: Atwood writes of the Instrument that “when finally brought through the natural Alembic, and returned, it constitutes the natural Alembic” [III.1 ¶61]. Two readings are possible. On one, the natural Alembic is the passage through which the impure Instrument goes and returns. On the other, the Instrument itself becomes the natural Alembic. The repeated phrase may be a printing slip, so the text leaves this open.

E1171.summary: The vital fire of the natural life, which when fermented and opened frees the celestial Life and Light; in Eudoxus, the fire the Stone sympathizes with.
E1171.body:
**Atwood (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer):** the natural fire is the vital fire of the natural life. Fermented by the same life from another, it is opened and “sets free the celestial Life and Light” [APP ¶38].

**Eudoxus (quoted):** the Stone, an Astral Fire, sympathizes with Natural Fire, and “the igneous spirit of the natural fire is corporified in the substances which are analogous to it” [IV.3 ¶16]. The Stone grows in an 'Elementary Fire' geometrically proportioned to it [IV.3 ¶16]. The text does not say that Natural Fire and Elementary Fire are the same.

E1172.summary: Geber's term for a natural unfitness for the work, caused by defects of body or of soul.
E1172.body: Atwood reports Geber's term for a natural incapacity for the work, caused by bodily defects or defects of soul: “Natural Impotency, he asserts, is manifold” [III.4 ¶3].

E1173.summary: In Crollius, the agent that separates each mystery into its own receptacle and frees the medicine from impure outside elements.
E1173.body: Crollius (quoted): “the natural inbred chemist teaches to segregate every mystery into its own reservacle” [III.1 ¶10]. It frees the medicine from impure external elements. The text gives no further definition. The phrase apparently names an inner, natural agent of separation, though what exactly it is stays open.

E1174.summary: Man's 'phantasic' Spirit, the vestibule of Reason, which in man matches the Ether in the universe; it is imperfect and its Light is hidden.
E1174.body: Atwood: “for what the natural intelligent Spirit is in man, that Ether is in the universe” [III.1 ¶5]. She calls it 'phantasic' and the vestibule of Reason [III.1 ¶5]. Earlier chapters have shown “the imperfection of the natural Spirit in his world, the occultation of its Light” [III.1 ¶4].

E1175.summary: The soul's ordinary, unregenerate state, where no lasting leader rules and passing motives take control.
E1175.body: Atwood: “the government of the natural life is oligarchical, almost an anarchy” [II.4 ¶38]. In this state no permanent leader rules and passing motives take control.

E1176.summary: Ordinary reason: needed at the threshold but dull and idle in the work, unable to purify the phantastic Spirit; it is the image of the supernatural reason.
E1176.body:
Atwood treats natural reason as necessary but only an aid at the threshold. In the work itself it is dull and inoperative [III.1 ¶20–21]. It cannot purify the phantastic Spirit: “But the natural Intellect cannot do this” [III.1 ¶20]. It is the image of the higher faculty: “these things which the natural reason as an image enacts theoretically, this supernatural reason is said to do as an archetype essentially” [III.1 ¶21].

= **iron key**: “as it were an iron key, intended to unlock the golden treasury of light within” [III.1 ¶13].

E1177.summary: What the avaricious are afraid to 'interposit'; Atwood glosses this as giving up the life of selfhood and turning the product to a benevolent and truthful end.
E1177.body: In the passage from Geber, on the avaricious: “but are afraid to interposit the necessary charges” [III.4 ¶3]. In Geber's wording the failure is covetousness of money. Atwood reinterprets the charges in her own voice: “i.e., to abandon the life of selfhood, and return the product to a benevolent and truthful end” [III.4 ¶6]. Her gloss apparently makes the cost moral and inward rather than financial.

E1178.summary: A Lion said to be born of 'her foam' and identified with what the sentence before describes; the exact referent is unclear.
E1178.body: Atwood: “and this is that Nemean Lion said to be born of her foam” [IV.1 ¶29]. The Lion is identified with what the sentence before describes. It is unclear from the record what that is, and whose foam is meant.

E1179.summary: Philosophers Atwood cites for a hidden Principle of Universal Science and for teaching principles while keeping silent on the Practice.
E1179.body:
Atwood cites them as support for a latent Principle of Universal Science that can be known under certain conditions [II.1 ¶39]. They spoke of Principles and of how the mind proceeds while avoiding the Practice; their images stir inward faith [III.2 ¶46].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she qualifies this. They set out principles scientifically and went through long-perfected Initiation, but did not declare the inner experience of the Mystae and Teleioi. They kept to psychological investigation, and Behmen surpassed them here [APP ¶122].

E1180.summary: A region reached after the first barriers, where one must choose Light; the text does not explain it further.
E1180.body: Atwood mentions “approaching to the Nether confines, to make choice of Light” [IV.1 ¶25]. The region comes after the first barriers. The text does not explain it further.

E1181.summary: The moment when extremes are present and Light springs forth out of the abyssal Darkness.
E1181.body: Atwood: “extremes are said to be present at the new birth, when Light springs forth to manifestation out of the abyssal Darkness” [III.2 ¶56].

E1182.summary: The new beginning that the former life, all but destroyed, draws to itself through a new seed.
E1182.body: Atwood describes the former life, nearly annihilated, “which at length, in its extreme exigence, draws a new seed to begin a New Generation” [III.2 ¶28]. The new start comes out of the extreme destruction of the old.

E1183.summary: Atwood's name for the agent of mesmerism, which she identifies with the Common Soul.
E1183.body: Atwood uses this name for the agent at work in mesmerism and identifies it with the Common Soul: “our New Imponderable, for it is the Common Soul” [II.2 ¶18].

E1184.summary: What arises once the evil of Original Sin is overcome by subtle stratagems; its quintessential virtue is the Corner Stone.
E1184.body: Atwood: “The evil of the Original Sin being overcome by so many subtle stratagems, the New Life thence arises” [III.1 ¶66]. Its quintessential virtue is the Corner Stone [III.1 ¶66].

E1185.summary: The New Light of Alchemy, cited as one of the sources of a summary passage.
E1185.body: Cited as one of the sources of the summary passage [I.2 ¶33]; the footnote names it as the *New Light of Alchemy* [I.2 n36].

E1186.summary: In Boehme, the regenerate inner seer who looks into the astral birth, as opposed to the external man.
E1186.body: Boehme (quoted): “for the new man speculates into the midst of the astral birth or geniture” [III.2 ¶16]. The new man is contrasted with the external man, so the context suggests the regenerate inner seer.

E1187.summary: Cited as recognizing the possibility and not condemning the tradition; also used once for comparison.
E1187.body: Atwood cites Sir Isaac Newton as support: he recognized the possibility and did not condemn the tradition [I.1 ¶82]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is named for comparison only [APP ¶122].

forms: Night of Hippocrates / Day of Orpheus
E1188.summary: Paired images: the radical destruction leads back to the Night of Hippocrates and on into the Day of Orpheus.
E1188.body: Atwood calls the radical destruction “the way of the recedure to the Night of Hippocrates, leading thenceforth into the Day of Orpheus” [III.2 ¶28]. The text does not explain the two terms further. The context suggests a return to darkness that is followed by light.

E1189.summary: The state of the mind beholding Matter: it receives the formless and perceives obscurely, vastly, infinitely, feeling without understanding.
E1189.body: The passage opens: “When therefore the mind is in the Night of Matter” [III.2 ¶55]. In this state the mind suffers the reception of the formless and perceives obscurely, vastly, infinitely; it feels without understanding [III.2 ¶55]. The voice is unclear: the record does not show whether this is Atwood or a cited authority.

E1190.summary: An unnamed adept cited for the view that Venus's light alone is imperfect without the masculine tincture.
E1190.body: Atwood cites this unnamed adept in support. Venus's light alone is imperfect without the masculine tincture, though at that stage “the artist is rejoiced, and thinks perhaps his work is finished” [I.3 n49].

forms: a no less subtle than experienced adept
E1191.summary: An unnamed adept cited for water turning into air and back, and for the image of the old man swallowing gold or silver.
E1191.body: Atwood cites this unnamed adept to illustrate water turning into air and back again: “the central heat may change the water into air” [I.3 n31]. The adept also gives the image of the old man swallowing gold or silver [I.3 n31].

E1192.summary: Used as an illustration of the principle kept safe in the water through destruction, which then renews all things.
E1192.body: Atwood uses Noah to illustrate the principle preserved in the water through destruction, which renews all things: “as Noah in the Ark” [III.3 ¶71].

E1193.summary: In a quoted poem, the narrator's master, whose deathbed oath is the narrator's reason for veiling the secrets.
E1193.body: Inside the quoted poem, the narrator gives his master's deathbed charge as his reason for veiling: “At his death he made me sweare hym to, That all the secrets I schould never undoe” [III.1 ¶65].

E1194.summary: Coins struck from Lully's gold, about 10 ducats each, of the finest metal, with a marginal inscription said to mark their miraculous origin.
E1194.body: Atwood reports that from Lully's gold “a coinage of the gold was struck in pieces weighing about 10 ducats each, called Nobles of the Rose” [I.1 ¶47]. They were of the finest metal, and their marginal inscription was said to denote their miraculous origin [I.1 ¶47].

E1195.summary: In Parmenides, what neither mind nor speech can reach; in Hegel, the empty abstraction of pure Being; for the Kabalists, the primitive non-Being, the Cause of causes.
E1195.body:
The text quotes three distinct views.

**Parmenides:** Non-being is what neither mind can see nor speech reveal, “since, as of Being void, ‘Tis not the object of the mental eye” [III.2 ¶14].

**Hegel:** “this pure Being is no other than a pure abstraction, it is a term absolutely negative, which may also in its immediate conception be called non-Being” [III.2 ¶30]. So for Hegel pure Being = non-Being.

**The Kabalists (the Rabbi):** non-Being is not nothing in the ordinary sense. It is not produced “from nothing in the common-sense acceptation of that word; for Being could never be produced from non-Being (deficiently understood), but by non-Being they mean” [III.2 ¶32] something else. It cannot be conceived as cause or essence, “but yet is in fact the Cause of causes: it is that which we call the primitive non-Being; because it is anterior to the universe” [III.2 ¶32]. It is not corporeity: “by it we do not signify corporeity either, but that Principle or Wisdom on which it is founded” [III.2 ¶32]. It holds no distinction. Identities asserted: = Cause of causes; = Principle or Wisdom [III.2 ¶32].

The readings differ: Parmenides calls it unknowable, Hegel calls it an empty abstraction, and the Kabalists call it the Cause of causes and the Principle or Wisdom.
